problem: Social navigation datasets are mostly bird's-eye pedestrian trajectories that are small and lack first-person visual cues. Models trained on them need top-down cameras or LiDAR-derived views and only see positions and velocities.
motivation: A robot should navigate crowds using only an onboard depth camera, but first-person social navigation data is costly to collect and label at scale. Game engines can re-render existing top-down trajectories as first-person depth views and generate unlimited extra trajectories for pre-training.
key_idea: Re-render bird's-eye pedestrian trajectories in Unity as first-person depth views, pre-train on NavMesh-generated synthetic trajectories, and train an LSTM velocity-imitation model with next-depth-frame prediction as an auxiliary task.
insight: Pre-training on synthetic trajectories matters most for collision avoidance: without it collisions rise from 0.018 to 0.094, and with half the pre-training data they rise to 0.056. The auxiliary depth-forecasting task halves collisions (0.037 without it vs 0.018 with it) but slightly worsens FDE (0.34 vs 0.20). A history window of T=1 hurts overall performance (social score 0.051 vs 0.040).
method: First-person view generation: a Unity simulator replays BIWI bird's-eye trajectories with animated human models and stores per-agent, per-step first-person depth images, position, goal and velocity.
Data augmentation: Unity NavMesh agents walk to random goals, giving 6,000 artificial trajectories on the two maps. These do not guarantee social behavior and are used only for pre-training.
Depth preprocessing: depth is normalized by d_max = 7 m and clipped to 1 beyond range. Positions and goals are normalized across maps.
Architecture: a shared CNN+MLP encodes each of T=10 depth frames, and a shared MLP embeds position and goal. The concatenated features feed a 2-layer LSTM whose last hidden state drives two heads.
Head 1 (velocity): an MLP predicts the next velocity (vx, vy) by imitating the human trajectory.
Head 2 (auxiliary): predicts the next depth frame D_{t+1}.
Loss: L = L_v + k·L_D with k=0.1, both squared errors. A weight c=2 is applied when the minimum depth reading is below β (nearby obstacle).
Training: pre-train 15 epochs on synthetic trajectories (lr 1e-3), then fine-tune 10 epochs on the BIWI-derived data (lr 1e-4), with a 9/1 train/eval split.

setting.training_data: Unity re-rendering of BIWI ETH/Hotel trajectories (787 agents) plus 6,000 synthetic NavMesh trajectories for pre-training
setting.observation: first-person depth image (320x240, 135° FOV, 7 m range) history T=10, plus agent position and goal coordinates
setting.simulator: Unity (custom, recreated BIWI ETH and Hotel maps)
setting.privileged: none for the model beyond the position and goal coordinates; the SFM baseline uses other agents' positions and velocities, and NaviGAN uses coordinate-level oracle information

numbers.eval_set_note: random 1/10 held-out trajectories of BIWI ETH/Hotel re-created in Unity
numbers.backbone: CNN + LSTM, trained from scratch (synthetic pre-training + fine-tune)

numbers_note: Only a custom Unity-recreated BIWI benchmark, with no standard navigation benchmark. The split is a random 10% hold-out. The GT social score is 0.034.
results: DeepSocNav gets the best social score (0.040) and collisions (0.018) with 100% success, beating SFM (0.054, 0.037) and RVO (0.067). It is worse than SFM on ADE and FDE (0.24/0.34 vs 0.20/0.16) but far better than NaviGAN (0.43/0.74).
limitations: Evaluated only on the small BIWI ETH/Hotel scenes recreated in simulation, with no real-robot tests and no standard benchmarks.
Trajectory-similarity metrics (ADE/FDE) are worse than SFM, and the auxiliary task trades off FDE.
Synthetic pre-training trajectories are not social, and the evaluation is a workshop-level study with a single seed and no statistics.
